scope: Substances: the 840 values graded unverified in 111 records
method: One researcher per batch proposed values from sources it opened; one skeptic per batch opened every source and accepted, corrected or rejected each.

accepted.source: Anthony, Bideaux, Bladh & Nichols, Handbook of Mineralogy, 'Lizardite' (Mineral Data Publishing, 2001, v1.2), Optical Properties: alpha 1.538-1.554, beta 1.546-1.560, gamma 1.546-1.560; name for the type locality, the Lizard complex, Cornwall; chemical analysis (1) and X-ray pattern from Kennack Cove. https://www.handbookofmineralogy.org/pdfs/lizardite.pdf
accepted.derivation: n = mean of the mid-range principal indices = (1.546 + 1.553 + 1.553) / 3 = 1.5507, rounded 1.551. F0 = ((n-1)/(n+1))^2 = 0.0467 (was 0.0479 at 1.56).
accepted.note: Checked against the PDF: the indices, the Kennack Cove analysis and the type-locality naming are all as stated. Corrected: the proposal gave the F0 values as 0.0468 and 0.0475. Recomputed, F0 is 0.0467 at 1.551 and 0.0479 at 1.56. The Handbook does not say the Lizard rock is mainly lizardite. That is an inference from the naming and the Kennack Cove analysis. It is reasonable, but it is not stated. Bastite, chrysotile and the hematite of the red variety are left out.

accepted.source: 'Decoding the nanoscale porosity in serpentinites from multidimensional electron microscopy and discrete element modelling', Contributions to Mineralogy and Petrology 178(11), published 17 Oct 2023, PMC11008076: in lizardite-dominated serpentinites, the average porosity of the FIB-SEM excavated volumes is 0.4 +/- 0.07 %, 0.7 +/- 0.08 % and 0.2 +/- 0.05 %; TEM foils average 1-3 %; nanopores are mostly under 10 nm, with some up to 100 nm. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11008076/
accepted.note: Corrected: the paper is from 2023 in Contrib. Mineral. Petrol. 178(11), not 2024. 0.005 lies inside the 0.002-0.007 FIB-SEM range. This is evidence for the rock type only. The samples are from ODP Leg 209 Site 1274 on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge and the Roragen complex in Norway, not from the Lizard. The paper measures total nanoporosity and does not separate connected (open) porosity. Its models suggest the pores connect but warn that natural rock may be less connected. So as an open porosity this value is an upper-leaning estimate.

accepted.source: Amgueddfa Cymru, Mineralogy of Wales database, 'Antigorite': the serpentinized rocks of the New Harbour Group, Anglesey, 'were once referred to as Mona Marble'; antigorite SW of Llanfechell; Maltman (1977) mentions antigorite with lizardite in serpentinite from Holy Island. https://museum.wales/mineralogy-of-wales/database/?mineral=15&name=Antigorite . Handbook of Mineralogy 'Antigorite' (alpha 1.558-1.567, beta 1.565, gamma 1.562-1.574) https://www.handbookofmineralogy.org/pdfs/antigorite.pdf and 'Lizardite' (alpha 1.538-1.554, beta and gamma 1.546-1.560) https://www.handbookofmineralogy.org/pdfs/lizardite.pdf
accepted.note: Checked: all the indices and museum statements are as cited, and the arithmetic holds. The equal weighting is an assumption. The museum page records the two serpentines together only in Holy Island serpentinite, which is New Harbour Group, and gives no proportions. Calcite or dolomite in the veins and breccia matrix (n about 1.60) is left out. A carbonate-rich shaft would read higher. If a shaft is known to be antigorite-only, 1.565 applies.

accepted.source: Handbook of Mineralogy (Mineral Data Publishing 2001): Quartz omega 1.544, epsilon 1.553 https://www.handbookofmineralogy.org/pdfs/quartz.pdf ; Microcline alpha 1.514-1.529, beta 1.518-1.533, gamma 1.521-1.539 https://www.handbookofmineralogy.org/pdfs/microcline.pdf ; Albite alpha 1.526-1.530, beta 1.531-1.533, gamma 1.534-1.541 https://www.handbookofmineralogy.org/pdfs/albite.pdf
accepted.derivation: quartz (2x1.544 + 1.553)/3 = 1.547; microcline (1.5215 + 1.5255 + 1.530)/3 = 1.526; albite (1.528 + 1.532 + 1.5375)/3 = 1.5325; equal weights give 1.535; a few per cent of biotite (n about 1.6) adds about 0.003, so rounded to 1.54. F0 = 0.0452 (was 0.0465 at 1.55).
accepted.note: Checked: all the Handbook indices match and the arithmetic holds. The mix is unweighted because no modal analysis was found. Plagioclase in granite is often oligoclase rather than pure albite, and oligoclase has a higher index. That also pushes the value toward 1.54 rather than 1.535, so the rounded value stands.

accepted.source: Handbook of Mineralogy: Quartz, Microcline, Albite PDFs (as for Peterhead). The Open University Virtual Microscope, 'Two mica granite - Aberdeen', Rubislaw quarry: quartz intergrown with altered plagioclase and microcline, with fox-brown biotite and muscovite. https://www.virtualmicroscope.org/content/two-mica-granite-aberdeen
accepted.derivation: Quartz 1.547, microcline 1.526 and albite 1.5325 weighted equally give 1.535. The muscovite and biotite of this two-mica granite (n about 1.56-1.60) raise it to about 1.54.
accepted.note: Checked: the mineral list on the Virtual Microscope page for a Rubislaw quarry specimen matches, and it gives no modal proportions. The plagioclase is described only as 'altered plagioclase', not as albite-oligoclase. The albite indices stand in for it. A more calcic plagioclase would only support rounding up to 1.54.

accepted.source: British Geological Survey / Historic Environment Scotland, Building Stone Database for Scotland, 'Peterhead Granite' (record 10134): grain size 'Coarse crystalline (2 to 16 mm)', texture 'Weakly porphyritic', colour 'Medium greyish pink', water absorption 'Very low'. https://webservices.bgs.ac.uk/buildingstone/buildingstones/10134
accepted.derivation: geometric centre of the BGS grain class: sqrt(2 x 16) = 5.66 mm, rounded 5.7 mm
accepted.note: Checked: the record fields are as quoted. The value is a class centre, not a measured grain size, and the weakly porphyritic feldspar phenocrysts are larger. It confirms the old 6 mm.

accepted.source: British Geological Survey / Historic Environment Scotland, Building Stone Database for Scotland, 'Aberdeen Granite' (record 10159): grain size 'Medium crystalline (0.25 to 2 mm) to coarse crystalline (2 to 16 mm)', colour 'Medium grey to dark grey and pinkish grey to pink', key constituent muscovite, texture 'Tectonically foliated', water absorption 'Very low'. https://webservices.bgs.ac.uk/buildingstone/buildingstones/10159
accepted.derivation: geometric centre of the BGS range: sqrt(0.25 x 16) = 2.0 mm
accepted.note: Checked: the fields are as quoted. The BGS record names no quarries and does not mention Rubislaw, saying only 'numerous quarries' in and near Aberdeen. The link to Rubislaw rests on the Virtual Microscope's Rubislaw specimen being this pluton's two-mica granite. The value is a range centre, not a measurement, and confirms the old 2 mm.

accepted.source: Dorset Building Stone, 'Upper Purbeck (Purbeck Marble)': the thin beds are 'usually of less than 12" (.3 m) in thickness but rarely as much as 1.00 m or more'; maximum thicknesses: Blue bed 0.11 m, Green bed 0.81 m, Grey bed 0.38 m, Pre-Unio grey bed 0.20 m; the Green bed 'not uncommonly' oxidises to red. https://www.dorsetbuildingstone.org/upper-purbeck-purbeck-marble.html . Wikipedia, 'Purbeck Marble': beds 'never more than 1.2 m thick and are often much thinner'. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Purbeck_Marble
accepted.note: Checked. Clarified: 0.3 m is the usual upper limit ('usually of less than 12 in'), not a typical thickness. Most beds are thinner, so 300 mm is the top of the usual range. The per-bed figures are maxima. Neither cited page says that shafts were cut from single beds, so that remains an inference. The Green bed (up to 810 mm, and it can oxidise red) is the exception if a shaft is read as that bed.

accepted.source: A. F. Hallimond, 'Pyroxenes, amphibole, and mica from the Tiree marble', Mineralogical Magazine 28 (1947) 230-243. p.230: a 'fine-grained, severely crushed limestone'; dark green patches 'usually do not exceed half an inch across and are often much smaller'. p.231: pyroxene (coccolite) grains or aggregates 'usually less than 1/3 of an inch across' in pink porcellanous calcite. p.232: in the calc-gneiss, dark silicate grains up to 1/3 inch and an aggregate about 3 in long. Table I: diopside alpha 1.673, beta 1.679, gamma 1.699, sp. gr. 3.29. https://www.rruff.net/doclib/MinMag/Volume_28/28-199-230.pdf
accepted.derivation: 1/3 in x 25.4 mm/in = 8.47 mm, rounded 8.5 mm; the stated usual upper size of the dark pyroxene grains
accepted.note: Checked: every quotation and the Table I values are as stated. Caveat: 8.5 mm is an upper bound. The paper says the grains are 'usually less than' 1/3 inch and the patches 'often much smaller'. It is not a typical size, and it is not the finest structure in the strict sense. A shader should treat it as the upper end of the visible dark-grain scale. The other records use range centres, so this one sits on a different basis. The pyroxene-marble specimen is from the NE end of the Balephetrish shore section, and the calc-gneiss specimen is from the pink marble quarry.

No measured colour was found. The sources say 'dark grey' (North Pennines AONB leaflet) or 'black, bituminous' (Wikipedia), with white coral sections.

No measured colour was found. Descriptions are 'light beige/white' (Britannicus Stone), 'pale, buff-grey' (Building Conservation) and 'fine cream-coloured' (Canterbury AHS). Britannicus's factsheet was not opened.

No measured colour was found. Sources say 'grey to black with white and pink veins of calcite' (The Architectural Forum) and 'dark grey to black ... red and white veining' (Building Conservation). These suggest a darker ground than the record's L*38.
No measured colour was found. Sources say 'predominantly white with greenish veining and mottling' (Building Conservation) and white with yellow-green serpentine.
No measured colour was found. Hallimond (1947) describes 'pink porcellanous calcite' with dark pistachio-green pyroxene, which is qualitative only.
No measured colour was found. Sources say 'variegated dark green, white veined serpentinite' (Building Conservation), and Museum Wales notes green and purple serpentinite.

stillUnverified.record: iona-marble, tiree-marble, hopton-wood, frosterley-marble, ashburton-marble, purbeck-marble
stillUnverified.why: Not unverified: these are already graded derived from calcite (cream-marble F0). The Handbook of Mineralogy calcite omega 1.658, epsilon 1.486 was opened and supports the calcite basis, so no change is proposed.
No measured porosity for Peterhead granite was found. BGS gives only 'Water absorption: Very low', and its numeric class limits could not be found. 0.006 is plausible for granite but has no source.

No measured porosity was found. BGS (Aberdeen Granite) says 'Very low' water absorption, qualitatively. A Scottish hygrothermal-data paper (Materials and Structures 2021, s11527-021-01759-x) may hold granite data, but Springer's login redirect blocked it.
No number was found. Dorset Building Stone calls Purbeck Marble 'not at all porous' in thin section, which argues the record's 0.02 is too high. The BRE data are only on request from Haysom.
No measurement of Frosterley marble's porosity was found.

A search snippet gave 'porosity 7.6 %, saturation coefficient 0.60' for Hopton Wood, probably BRE data (Leary 1983, 'The building limestones of the British Isles'). The pages holding it (stonecontact.com, Springer) returned 403 or a login redirect, so it could not be read and is not cited. If confirmed, 0.076 would replace 0.06.
No measurement of Ashburton marble's porosity was found.
No measurement of Iona marble's porosity was found.
No measurement of Tiree marble's porosity was found.
No measurement of Mona Marble's porosity was found. The serpentinite nanoporosity study (PMC11008076, 0.2-0.7 % by FIB-SEM) supports 0.005 for the rock type only, and was used for the Lizard record.
No published grain or vein scale for Lizard serpentine was found.
Granite has no bedding. 1000 mm stands for colour banding or schlieren at shaft scale, and no source gives it.
BGS calls the Aberdeen Granite 'tectonically foliated' and the Virtual Microscope notes 'biotite-rich patches', but neither gives a scale.

Grain is the Viviparus shells. The only size opened is for Sussex species (V. infracretacicus 10 x 4-5 mm, V. fluviorum 25 x 10-12 mm; Dorset Building Stone, Wimborne Minster). Purbeck's V. cariniferus has a snippet figure of '6-8 mm diameter' whose source could not be opened.

Grain is the section of the coral Dibunophyllum bipartitum. A figure of 7-10 mm for the axial structure came from a search snippet only (ResearchGate 403), and the whole corallite diameter was not found. The North Pennines AONB leaflet puts the Frosterley Marble layer at 'up to a metre thick' in the Great Limestone. That bounds the stone but is not the scale of structure on the face.
No crinoid ossicle or shell size was found. Britannicus gives slabs of about 1.4 m x 1.0 m, which is a block size, not a structure scale.
No fossil or vein-network scale was found.
No grain or streak scale was found. The quarry vein is about 7 m wide (Visit Mull & Iona, snippet only), which bounds block size only.
Hallimond (1947) records gneiss-like aggregates about 3 in (76 mm) long and 'locally ... pieces of dark gneiss-like rock of much larger size', but no banding scale. The 300 mm is still unsourced.
No breccia clast or vein scale for Mona Marble was found.

No published length-to-width ratio of veining, banding or fossils was found for any of the ten stones. It is an appearance parameter and would need image measurement of a real slab, or a 'design' grade.

The cited Candela et al. 2012 range (0.6-0.8) is for fault-surface topography, not for the albedo pattern of a polished decorative stone. No material-specific value was found, so it stays unverified (or becomes 'design').
No published measurement of across-face albedo or roughness variation was found for any of these stones. These need image or gloss measurements of real slabs, or a 'design' grade.

No measured wetting depth was found. For polished dense stones with very low absorption it is an engineering judgement. The one sourced lead is Hopton Wood's probably higher porosity (above), and it could not be confirmed.

accepted.source: BRE (Building Research Establishment), 'Monks Park Limestone: Technical Data Sheet', Monks Park Mine, Corsham, Wilts, compiled September 1997 (tests at BRE 1996; porosity method Note 3 = prEN 1341 / BRE 141), Test Results table, 'Porosity and Water Absorption', pp. 3-4, https://bregroup.com/documents/311572/1309416/Monks+Park+Limestone.pdf/031955ac-5182-4710-370d-33f40c2466b2
accepted.derivation: 23.8 % as a fraction
accepted.note: Verified on the sheet. Porosity 23.8 % is on p. 3. The saturation coefficient of 0.85, the water absorption of 10.3 % by weight and the bulk density of 2066 kg/m3 (labelled 'bulk specific gravity') are on p. 4, not p. 3. The sheet calls the stone 'a fine-grained, buff coloured stone' and an oolitic limestone of the Great Oolite. It says three beds tested earlier had similar porosity and water absorption.

accepted.source: MuseeVision/Docs/Stages/albion.md §3.1 Coursing (BandCuts): 'every 1.20 one red course of 0.30 and three buff of 0.30'; §3.10 maps albion.wall.buff to accent.bath-stone
accepted.note: Verified in albion.md lines 119-122 and 322. The value is the height of the designed buff ashlar course, not a natural bed, and 'design' is the honest grade. BRE's Monks Park sheet (p. 2) says the stone is worked in galleries about 6 m high and seems to be divided into 'four or more beds'. A 0.30 m block therefore shows no natural bed.

accepted.source: Lott G.K. & Cooper A.H. (2005) 'The building limestones of the Upper Permian, Cadeby Formation (Magnesian Limestone) of Yorkshire', British Geological Survey Internal Report IR/05/048, Table 3 'Typical porosities in Cadeby Formation limestones (BGS archive data 1931)', p. 13 (sandy Mansfield facies described on p. 12), https://nora.nerc.ac.uk/504662/1/IR05048.pdf
accepted.derivation: 19.7 % as a fraction
accepted.note: Verified. Table 3 is on p. 13, not pp. 12-13, and lists Mansfield White at 19.7 % with a 'crystalline' fabric. It gives no figure for Mansfield Red, so the value stands in from the white variety of the same sandy facies. On p. 12 BGS says both were produced commercially as 'Mansfield Red and White stone' from the sandy facies, and that the last quarry closed in 2004. On p. 13 it says the best building limestones range from 19 % to 25 %. The data are 1931 archive values, so the grade is 'secondary'.

accepted.source: Handbook of Mineralogy (Mineral Data Publishing): Quartz, Uniaxial (+), omega 1.544, epsilon 1.553, https://www.handbookofmineralogy.org/pdfs/quartz.pdf ; Dolomite, Uniaxial (-), omega 1.679, epsilon 1.500, https://www.handbookofmineralogy.org/pdfs/dolomite.pdf ; quartz sand 'up to 50%': Wikipedia 'Mansfield stone' citing Lott 2001 p. 106, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mansfield_stone ; detrital sand 'up to 80% by volume' in the Mansfield facies, carbonate mean 54.35 % CaCO3 and 45.65 % MgCO3: BGS IR/05/048 p. 12, https://nora.nerc.ac.uk/504662/1/IR05048.pdf
accepted.derivation: For grains in random orientations, F0 = 0.5 R(n_o) + 0.5 <R(n_e(theta))> over the sphere, with R(n) = ((n-1)/(n+1))^2 and 1/n_e(theta)^2 = cos^2/n_o^2 + sin^2/n_e^2. This gives quartz F0 = 0.04613 and dolomite F0 = 0.05581; I rechecked both by Simpson's rule. A 50:50 mix gives F0 = 0.05097, so n = (1+sqrt F0)/(1-sqrt F0) = 1.583. An 80:20 mix gives F0 = 0.04806, so n = 1.562. The same method gives F0 = 0.0533 for calcite (1.658, 1.486), which matches cream-marble.json.
accepted.note: Corrected. The value 1.583 checks out, but at 80 % sand the index is 1.562, not the proposed min of 1.560. Caveat: both sources give only a maximum sand content ('up to'). The 50 % end is therefore a chosen reading, not a measured lower bound on the sand. A less sandy block would sit above 1.583, up to about 1.619 for pure dolomite. Porosity and the red iron-oxide colouring are left out. A modal count of a Mansfield Red thin section would fix the mix.

accepted.source: MuseeVision/Docs/Stages/albion.md §3.1 Coursing (BandCuts): 'every 1.20 one red course of 0.30'; §3.10 maps albion.wall.red to accent.mansfield-red
accepted.note: Verified in albion.md. The value is the height of the designed red course, graded as design. The stone's own structure is current (cross) bedding, commonly cut by greenish-grey clay seams (Wikipedia 'Mansfield stone', citing Lott 2001 p. 106), and no opened source measures it. I did not open the 'Language of Stone' blog cited in the proposal, so it is left out.

accepted.source: Levantina, 'Negro Marquina Marmol / Marble: Ficha tecnica | Technical file' (March 2025), p. 03 table: Porosidad abierta / Open porosity 0.3 % (UNE-EN 1936); water absorption 0.1 % (UNE-EN 13755); apparent density 2700 kg/m3; p. 04: ASTM C 97-09 absorption 0.13 %, bulk specific gravity 2699 kg/m3, https://www.levantina.com/files/74b9d95b0cbb53ef86851135a9b72c53/20004873/1/12-negro-marquina-ficha-v2.pdf
accepted.derivation: 0.3 % as a fraction
accepted.note: Verified. The ASTM figures are on p. 04 of the sheet, not p. 03. The sheet's 'Nature' section describes the stone as a limestone biomicrite with rudist and oyster (ostreid) remains, about 115 Ma (early Aptian to late Albian, Early Cretaceous), with calcite veins and scattered fossils. Its UNE-EN 12407 petrographic name is 'Caliza / Limestone'.

accepted.source: Les Carrieres de la Pierre Bleue Belge SA (Soignies), 'Belgian Blue Stone' brochure (2022), Technical characteristics table, p. 11: Porosity 0.24 % vol, standard deviation 0.15, n = 244 (NBN EN 1936:2007); water absorption 0.10 % m (NBN EN 13755:2008); apparent bulk density 2690 kg/m3; capillary absorption (NBN EN 1925) 'Not applicable, due to the low porosity of the stone', https://www.pierrebleuebelge.be/en/wp-content/uploads/sites/3/2022/12/Pierre-Bleue-Belge-Brochure-Belgian-Blue-Stone.pdf
accepted.derivation: 0.24 % by volume as a fraction
accepted.note: Verified. It agrees with UBAtc ATG 00/H724 (S.A. Carrieres du Hainaut, Soignies, 2000): porosity under vacuum 0.28 % vol, s = 0.13, n = 131 (NBN B24-213), averaged over the Soignies and Condroz basins, https://api.butgb-ubatc.be/api/public/file/ATG00H724F_000114A_1.pdf. I did not open Pereira et al. 2015, so it is dropped from the note.

accepted.source: Debout L. & Denayer J. (2018) 'Palaeoecology of the Upper Tournaisian (Mississippian) crinoidal limestones from South Belgium', Geologica Belgica 21(3-4):111-127: in the Soignies Member at the Gauthier-Wincqz quarry 'The columnal diameter fluctuates between 0.2 to 10 mm'; histograms polymodal (Fig. 11), https://popups.uliege.be/1374-8505/index.php?id=5991

The paper gives the 0.2 to 10 mm range for the Soignies Member beds, which it names as the Gros dur, Cul de Poupli, Banc dit de 3 metres and so on, the same beds as the ATG quarry log. accepted.source: Granital Siena s.r.l., 'Cave di marmo Giallo Siena: Giallo Siena Broccatello' data sheet (A.D. Arianna Losi, Marzo 2013; tests at the Marble Laboratory, Politecnico di Torino), physical-mechanical table: EN 1936-07 open porosity 0.24 % (st. dev. 0.09); EN 13755-08 water absorption 0.10 % (0.01); EN 1936-07 apparent density 2710 kg/m3, http://www.granitalsiena.com/pdf/giallo-siena-broccatello-marmo-granital-siena.pdf
accepted.derivation: 0.24 % as a fraction
accepted.note: Verified on the Broccatello variety from Sovicille (Siena). The macroscopic description reads 'The rock is compact but porous near the veins'. I did not open the Lithos Design listing, so it is dropped.

accepted.source: Granital Siena s.r.l., 'Giallo Siena Broccatello' data sheet (2013), microscopic description (EN 12407 and EN 12670): calcite > 95 % in straight anhedral crystals; 'The crystals vary from 60 to 900 um in some veins and patches of the mosaic'; macroscopic: 'medium-fine-grained', http://www.granitalsiena.com/pdf/giallo-siena-broccatello-marmo-granital-siena.pdf
accepted.derivation: Geometric mean of the stated crystal-size range: sqrt(0.06 mm x 0.9 mm) = 0.232 mm

The sheet's sentence (Italian: 'variano da 60 a 900 um in alcune venature e plaghe del mosaico') can be read as giving the range only for some veins and patches. accepted.source: Arel Stone (Turkey), 'Afyon Violet Marble' product technical data: porosity 0.2 %, water absorption 0.1 %, density 2.73 g/cm3, http://www.arelstone.com/en/DetayAfyonMenekse.aspx
accepted.derivation: 0.2 % as a fraction
accepted.note: Verified on the page, which names no test standard. The identity of Afyon Violet with pavonazzetto rests on the project's own Palette.json (accent.pavonazzetto realMaterial: 'traded today as Afyon violet', Afyon-Iscehisar, the site of the ancient Docimium quarries). accepted.source: Handbook of Mineralogy (Mineral Data Publishing), Andesine, Biaxial (+): alpha 1.545-1.556, beta 1.548-1.558, gamma 1.552-1.563; 'widespread in igneous rocks of intermediate silica content, as syenites and andesites', https://www.handbookofmineralogy.org/pdfs/andesine.pdf ; ISPRA Museo, 'Porfido rosso antico': 'porfido andesitico-dacitico', phenocrysts 'principalmente di plagioclasio, con subordinati feldspato potassico e orneblenda', microcrystalline groundmass, secondary haematite and piemontite, https://www.isprambiente.gov.it/it/attivita/museo/collezioni-litomineralogiche/lito-reperti/porfido-rosso-antico
accepted.derivation: The mean of the three principal indices, each taken at the middle of its range: (1.5505 + 1.553 + 1.5575) / 3 = 1.554. The min and max are the lowest alpha and the highest gamma.
accepted.note: Corrected note. ISPRA names the phenocrysts only as plagioclase. The choice of andesine rests on the rock being andesitic-dacitic, and ISPRA gives no measured anorthite content. ISPRA does not mention quartz or say what the groundmass is made of. The proposal's claims about groundmass quartz and a mostly plagioclase groundmass are therefore removed. Subordinate K-feldspar and hornblende, and the haematite and piemontite, are left out and would shift the index slightly.

accepted.source: Li L., Zhao J., Li J., Guo J. (2026) 'Provenance study of Eastern Zhou Dynasty (770-256 BC) stone chimes excavated from the Chu territory, China', Frontiers in Earth Science 14:1812060, doi:10.3389/feart.2026.1812060: Lingbi samples Lbs01 0.02-0.1 mm, Lbs02 0.01-0.05 mm, Lbs03 0.01-0.1 mm, 'calcite grains in mosaic contact, with minimal mineral impurities', https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/earth-science/articles/10.3389/feart.2026.1812060/full

F0_antigorite = ((1.565-1)/(1.565+1))^2 = 0.04852. F0_mix = 0.512 x 0.0533 + 0.488 x 0.04852 = 0.05097. n = (1+sqrt(F0))/(1-sqrt(F0)) = 1.583. The ends of the CaO range give 1.582 and 1.585.

The cited CITESwoodID page (opened) says only that storied structure is present, '5 per axial millimetre', without naming which elements are storied; in Dalbergia it can be the axial parenchyma, vessel elements and fibres, with the rays storied only in part. The only ray-height statement the source makes is 'Large rays commonly less than 1 mm high'. Even if the premise held, 1/5 mm is an upper bound, and the proposal stores it as the value. Wrong quantity. MatterWood.h defines rayWidth as 'A fleck's width across the grain' on a quarter-sawn face, and Wood.ush uses it as the fleck's across-grain size on that face. On a radial face a ray's across-grain extent is its radial run (or, on a slightly off-radial cut, width / sin(angle)), not its tangential width of 22 um. The proposal's own note flags this mismatch. The Wu et al. (2022) figure itself is correct (multiseriate mean 22 um, 14-37 um), but it answers a different question.

The derivation does not follow from its sources. It claims the rays are 'only one cell wide', but Kim et al. (2009, opened) describe fusiform rays containing radial resin canals, 20 cells high on average, which are multiseriate. CITESwoodID (opened) notes that 'wider, light-colored rays can be observed at irregular intervals' on clean transverse sections, which contradicts 'cannot be seen by the naked eye'. Neither source states naked-eye invisibility. The value 0 may still be a reasonable design choice given the low contrast, but it is not derived from this anatomy. Keep it unverified, or derive a small area share from a measured ray volume proportion and set rayTone near 1.
